chapterThermodynamics high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on identifying the adiabatic curve on a P-V diagram by comparing slopes of adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric processes, which is thermodynamics.
subtopic 1Adiabatic Process
subtopic 2not assigned (one subtopic chosen)
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the adiabatic curve on a P-V diagram being steeper than the isothermal curve (slope -gamma P/V versus -P/V), a property of the adiabatic process.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
An ideal gas undergoes four different processes from the same initial state as shown in the figure below. Those processes are adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric. The curve which represents the adiabatic process among 1, 2, 3 and 4 is
  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3
  4. 4
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. (dPdV)adiabatic = -γ P
  2. (dPdV)isothermal = -P
  3. (dPdV)adiabatic > (dPdV)isothermal

→ the working concludes: unclear

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. Curve 1 is vertical (V constant), so it is isochoric.
  2. Curve 4 is horizontal (P constant), so it is isobaric.
  3. For the isothermal process PV = const, so dPdV = -PV.
  4. For the adiabatic process PVγ = const, so dPdV = -γPV.
  5. Since γ > 1, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal one from the same initial state.
  6. Curve 2 is steeper than curve 3, so curve 2 is adiabatic, which is option 2.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict

difficultymedium · 2 steps
stepsEliminate the straight lines: the vertical line (constant V) is isochoric and the horizontal line (constant P) is isobaric, leaving the two curves → Recall that the adiabatic slope dP/dV = -γ P/V is γ times the isothermal slope -P/V, so the adiabatic is the steeper of the two curves from the common initial point and pick that curve
why it is trickyThe work is identifying the isochoric and isobaric lines by sight, then using the γ-times-steeper slope relation to tell the adiabatic curve from the isothermal one.

subtopic 2PN Junction Diode Under Reverse Bias
why subtopic 1The answer depends on recognising that the two series diodes are both identically biased in circuits (a) and (c) but one forward- and one reverse-biased in circuit (b), so the drops are equal only when both share the same bias state.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
In the given circuits (a), (b) and (c), the potential drop across the two p-n junctions are equal in
  1. Circuit (a) only
  2. Circuit (b) only
  3. Circuit (c) only
  4. Both circuits (a) and (c)
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Potential drops across the p-n junctions will be same if either both junctions are forward biased or both junction are reverse biased.
  2. In figure (a) and (c), both junctions are forward biased therefore both have same potential.
  3. In figure (b) first junction is forward biased and second junction is reverse biased, so both junctions have different potential difference.

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. In circuit (a) both junctions are oriented P→ N in series, so the same current flows through both with the same bias; identical junctions give V1 = V2.
  2. In circuit (b) one junction is P→ N and the other N→ P, so one is forward biased and the other reverse biased; Vforward ≪ Vreverse, so the drops are unequal.
  3. In circuit (c) both junctions are oriented N→ P in series, so both have the same bias and V1 = V2.
  4. Equal drops occur in (a) and (c), which is option 4.

    READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
    Which one of the following statements is correct?
    1. The atrio-ventricular node (AVN) generates an action potential to stimulate atrial contraction
    2. The tricuspid and the bicuspid valves open due to the pressure exerted by the simultaneous contraction of the atria
    3. Blood moves freely from atrium to the ventricle during joint diastole.
    4. Increased ventricular pressure causes closing of the semilunar valves.
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
    1. Option (3) is the correct answer because during joint diastole, blood moves freely from atrium to ventricle as atrioventricular valve remain open during joint diastole.
    2. Option (4) is incorrect because decrease in ventricular pressure, during ventricular diastole closes semilunar valves to produce ‘dub’ heart sound.
    3. Option (1) is incorrect because SA node generates action potential to stimulate atrial contraction.
    4. Option (2) is incorrect because bicuspid and tricuspid valves open due to pressure exerted by blood present in atria and decrease in pressure in ventricles during ventricular diastole.

    → the working concludes: option 3

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
    1. Option 1 is false: the SA node, not the AV node, generates the action potential that stimulates atrial contraction.
    2. Option 2 is false: the tricuspid and bicuspid valves are already open during joint diastole; atrial systole only adds about 30% more blood.
    3. Option 4 is false: increased ventricular pressure closes the AV valves and opens the semilunar valves; semilunar valves close when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure.
    4. Option 3 is true: during joint diastole the AV valves are open, so blood moves freely from atria into ventricles, giving option 3.
    printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
    33 highagree
    difficultymedium · 3 steps
    stepsRecall the conduction pathway: the SA node, not the AV node, generates the action potential that triggers atrial contraction; reject option 1 → Recall the sequence of the cardiac cycle: the AV valves open during joint diastole, when atrial pressure exceeds falling ventricular pressure, so blood flows freely from atria to ventricles before atrial systole; check this against options 2 and 3 → Recall that the semilunar valves close when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation, not when it rises; reject option 4 and keep the remaining statement
    why it is trickyThe candidate recalls the conduction pathway and the pressure-driven valve events of the cardiac cycle, then checks four statements against them; each wrong statement swaps one detail.
    the catchThree of the statements are near-correct, each with one swapped term: AVN instead of SAN, valves opened by atrial contraction instead of during joint diastole, and increased instead of decreased ventricular pressure.
